course.title: Search & indexing at scale
course.description: Search and indexing reps for the retrieval part of a system-design interview: sizing an inverted index from documents and unique terms, what a multi-term AND merge walks, why the rarest posting list caps its hits and how leading with it cuts the work to a few probes, the candidate overfetch behind fan-out top-K and deep pages, how the refresh interval sets visibility lag, the physical writes segment merges add on top of ingest, budgeting two-phase (cascade) ranking, why fan-out multiplies replicas per shard when you size a search cluster, and how much RAM a vector index needs. Every drill is whole-number arithmetic with the conversions named (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes; per-mille = parts per thousand = x/1000), so you practise the reasoning, not the calculator.

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/01-inve.instructions:
**Skills:** search · storage  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "We are adding full-text search over 10,000,000 documents. Each document has about 120 unique terms and a compressed posting costs about 10 bytes. How big is the inverted index?"

**Why it works.** An inverted index maps every term to the list of documents that contain it. Each (document, unique term) pair is one posting — repeated occurrences of a term inside one document fold into the same posting — so the posting count is docs × unique terms per doc, and the footprint is postings × bytes per posting (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `postingsCount(docs, uniqueTermsPerDoc)` → `docs × uniqueTermsPerDoc`
- `invertedIndexBytes(docs, uniqueTermsPerDoc, bytesPerPosting)` → `docs × uniqueTermsPerDoc × bytesPerPosting`

**Worked example.** 10,000,000 docs × 120 unique terms = **1,200,000,000** postings.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/01-inve.explanation:
Text indexes are sized by postings, and postings multiply documents by terms.

For `invertedIndexBytes(10000000, 120, 10)`:
- postings: 10,000,000 docs × 120 unique terms = 1,200,000,000
- × 10 bytes each → **12,000,000,000 bytes** (12 GB)

The index can rival the text it covers, so posting compression sets the budget — module 05's `index-memory-fit` sizes a B-tree as rows × bytes per entry, while here the inverted multiplier is documents × TERMS.
hints: Count (document, distinct term) pairs, not documents — every pair is one entry in some term's posting list.
postings = docs × uniqueTermsPerDoc; bytes = docs × uniqueTermsPerDoc × bytesPerPosting.
Every unique term in a document contributes one posting, docs × uniqueTermsPerDoc — multiply by the bytes each posting costs for the index footprint

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/02-post.instructions:
**Skills:** search · query  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "A user searches for `the kubernetes sidecar` as an AND query. The three posting lists hold 2,000,000, 40,000 and 300 documents. How many postings does a naive merge walk, what is the largest number of documents that can match — and at most how many lookups does it take if the engine leads with the rarest list?"

**Why it works.** An AND query intersects sorted posting lists. A naive merge advances through every list once, so its work is the sum of the list lengths. A match must appear in every list, so the intersection can never be larger than the shortest list — which is why engines lead with the rarest term and skip through the long lists instead of walking them: each posting of the rarest list is looked up in the other lists (a skip-list or block seek, not a walk), and a candidate missing from one list need not be looked up in the rest, so in the worst case, when every candidate has to be checked in every list, the work is the shortest length times the number of other lists. `listLengths` is always a non-empty array of positive integers.

**Your task.** Export three functions:
- `mergeOps(listLengths)` → the sum of the array's lengths
- `maxPossibleHits(listLengths)` → the largest number of documents that can match all lists
- `skipProbes(listLengths)` → the most probes a rarest-first intersection can make into the other lists (every posting of the rarest list looked up in every other list)

**Worked example.** Lists of 2,000,000, 40,000 and 300 → at most **300** documents can match.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/02-post.explanation:
The merge pays for the common words; the rare word decides the answer.

For `mergeOps([2000000, 40000, 300])` — an AND over "the" (2,000,000), "kubernetes" (40,000) and "sidecar" (300):
- naive merge: 2,000,000 + 40,000 + 300 = **2,040,300** postings walked
- but `maxPossibleHits` is min(2,000,000, 40,000, 300) = 300 documents
- rarest first: at most 300 postings × 2 other lists = **600** probes instead of 2,040,300 steps

Lead with the rarest list and skip through the rest — module 08's `map-vs-nested-scan` compares n + q against n × q over two collections; here it is k sorted lists and the min-list ceiling that drives query planning.
hints: A document matches only if it appears in every list — think about which list caps the answer, and what a merge that touches every entry costs.
ops = Σ listLengths; hits ≤ min(listLengths). worst-case probes = min(listLengths) × (lists − 1).

A multi-term AND walks every posting list once, so add the list lengths — and the intersection can never exceed the shortest list, which is why engines iterate the rarest term first: at worst each of its postings is looked up in every other list, the shortest length times one less than the number of lists

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/03-fano.instructions:
**Skills:** search · sharding  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our search index is split across 20 shards. A user pages to page 50 with 10 hits per page. How many candidate documents do the shards send the coordinator to render those 10 results?"

**Why it works.** The coordinator cannot know which shard holds the global winners — the best hits might all live on one shard — so every shard must return its own top k and the coordinator merges shards × k candidates. Page p (pages count from 1) needs the global top k × p, so each shard must send k × p of its own, and the pile grows to shards × k × page.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `candidatesFetched(shards, k)` → `shards × k`
- `deepPageCandidates(shards, k, page)` → `shards × k × page`

**Worked example.** 20 shards × top 10 = **200** candidates for page 1.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/03-fano.explanation:
Deep pages are paid for on every shard.

For `deepPageCandidates(20, 10, 50)`:
- page 50 of 10 hits needs the global top 10 × 50 = 500
- each of the 20 shards must send its own 500
- 20 × 500 = **10,000** candidates for the 10 results shown

This is why engines cap page depth or switch to search-after cursors — module 07's `scatter-gather` counts the shard QUERIES issued, while this counts the RESULT overfetch per query; module 05's `offset-pagination-cost` is the single-node version, here multiplied by the shard count.
hints: Any single shard might hold every global winner, so no shard may send fewer than the whole page depth it could be asked to cover.
candidates = shards × k; deep page = shards × k × page.
Every shard must send back its own top k so the coordinator sees shards × k candidates — and page p forces each shard to send k × p, so the pile grows to shards × k × page

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/04-refr.instructions:
**Skills:** search · freshness  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our search cluster refreshes every 30 seconds and publishing each refresh takes about 5 seconds. Product wants to promise that new tickets are searchable 'right away'. What is the worst-case delay — and at 400 writes/s, how many documents does each refresh publish?"

**Why it works.** A near-real-time engine buffers new documents and only makes them visible at a refresh, which opens a new searchable segment. The unluckiest document arrives just after a refresh, so it waits the whole interval and then the time the refresh itself takes to publish the new segment (`commitSec`). A durable commit (flush/fsync) is a separate step and is not on the visibility path. Each refresh publishes every write that arrived during one interval.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `maxVisibilityLagSec(refreshIntervalSec, commitSec)` → `refreshIntervalSec + commitSec`
- `docsBufferedAtRefresh(writesPerSec, refreshIntervalSec)` → `writesPerSec × refreshIntervalSec`

**Worked example.** 400 writes/s × a 30 s interval = **12,000** documents published per refresh.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/04-refr.explanation:
Freshness is set by the refresh cadence, not by the write.

For `maxVisibilityLagSec(30, 5)`:
- the unluckiest document lands just after a refresh and waits the full 30 s interval
- plus the 5 s the refresh takes to publish → **35 s** before it is searchable

The freshness promise is the interval, not zero — module 09's `backlog-sla-threshold` turns a rate × SLA into a queue alert, while here the refresh CADENCE itself sets both the staleness and the batch size.
hints: Searchability happens at refresh boundaries, not at write time — picture the document that arrives a moment after one.
max lag = interval + publish time; buffered = writes/s × interval.

The unluckiest document lands just after a refresh, so its worst-case lag is the whole refresh interval plus the time the refresh takes to publish — and the buffer at each refresh holds writesPerSec × interval docs

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/05-segm.instructions:
**Skills:** search · io  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "We ingest 50 GB of new documents a day into a segment-based index, and each document is rewritten by about 3 merge passes over its life. How many bytes hit the SSDs per day — and how much disk does a merge that produces our largest, 30 GB segment occupy at its peak?"

**Why it works.** Segment-based (LSM-style) indexes write new data into small immutable segments and later merge them into larger ones; every merge pass rewrites the data once more, so physical writes are ingest × (1 + passes). A merge writes the new segment before it deletes the inputs, so for a while the inputs and the output both sit on disk — a peak footprint of twice the merged data, of which the inputs already occupy half (the free space the merge needs on top is 1×) (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `mergeWriteBytesPerDay(ingestBytesPerDay, mergePasses)` → `ingestBytesPerDay × (1 + mergePasses)`
- `mergeScratchBytes(largestSegmentBytes)` → `2 × largestSegmentBytes`

**Worked example.** Merging a 30,000,000,000-byte segment occupies **60,000,000,000** bytes (60 GB) on disk at its peak.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/05-segm.explanation:
The disks see the merges, not just the ingest.

For `mergeWriteBytesPerDay(50000000000, 3)`:
- 50 GB is written once on ingest
- and rewritten by each of 3 merge passes → 50 × (1 + 3)
- = **200,000,000,000 bytes** (200 GB) of physical writes per day

Size SSD endurance for the merges, not the ingest — module 05's `index-write-amplification` counts per-insert row × index writes, while here whole-corpus REWRITE passes plus the 2× peak footprint of each merge set the hardware.
hints: Immutable segments never change in place — combining them means writing the data again, and the inputs stay until the output is complete.
physical = ingest × (1 + passes); scratch = 2 × largest segment.
Each merge pass rewrites the data once more, so physical writes are ingest × (1 + passes) — and merging a segment needs the old and new copies on disk at once, twice its size on disk at the peak

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/06-rank.instructions:
**Skills:** search · latency  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Retrieval returns 100,000 candidates per query. A cheap scorer costs 2 µs per document; our learned ranker costs 400 µs per document. How do we afford the good model inside a few-hundred-millisecond budget?"

**Why it works.** A cascade scores every candidate with the cheap model, then rescores only the top rerank set with the expensive one. Total cost is candidates × cheap µs plus rerankCount × expensive µs, divided by 1000 to read milliseconds (1 ms = 1,000 µs). The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `scoringMs(candidates, scoreUsEach)` → `candidates × scoreUsEach ÷ 1000`
- `twoPhaseMs(candidates, cheapUsEach, rerankCount, expensiveUsEach)` → `(candidates × cheapUsEach + rerankCount × expensiveUsEach) ÷ 1000`

**Worked example.** 100,000 candidates × 20 µs ÷ 1000 = **2,000 ms** for a single-phase pass.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/06-rank.explanation:
Spend the expensive model only where it changes the answer.

For `twoPhaseMs(100000, 2, 200, 400)`:
- cheap pass: 100,000 × 2 µs = 200,000 µs = 200 ms
- heavy model on the top 200: 200 × 400 µs = 80,000 µs = 80 ms
- total → **280 ms**, against 100,000 × 400 µs = 40,000 ms scoring everything expensively

The cascade is the only way to afford good ranking — module 06's `batching-amortization` splits one batch into fixed + per-item cost, while here two scoring TIERS split the work: the retrieval/rerank budget.
hints: Not every candidate deserves the expensive model — what if the cheap model decides which few do?
ms = (candidates × cheap µs + rerank × expensive µs) ÷ 1000.
Phase one scores every candidate at the cheap per-item microseconds, phase two rescores only the rerank set at the expensive rate — add the two products and divide by 1000 for milliseconds

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/07-sear.instructions:
**Skills:** search · capacity  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "The index has 12 shards and we expect 3,000 search queries/s at peak. One replica of one shard sustains 400 QPS, and we run one shard replica per node. How many nodes does the cluster need?"

**Why it works.** Under fan-out every query is sent to every shard, so each shard sees the FULL query rate — sharding splits the data, never the query load. Each shard therefore needs enough replicas to carry all of it on its own: ceil(queryQps ÷ perReplicaQps), rounded up because a fraction of a replica cannot be deployed. The cluster is shards × replicas per shard nodes.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `replicasPerShard(queryQps, perReplicaQps)` → `Math.ceil(queryQps / perReplicaQps)`
- `searchNodes(shards, queryQps, perReplicaQps)` → `shards × replicasPerShard(queryQps, perReplicaQps)`

**Worked example.** 3,000 QPS ÷ 400 per replica = 7.5, rounded up → **8** replicas per shard.
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/07-sear.explanation:
Fan-out makes replicas multiply per shard instead of dividing the load.

For `searchNodes(12, 3000, 400)`:
- every query touches every shard, so each shard group must sustain all 3,000 QPS
- replicas per shard: ceil(3,000 ÷ 400) = ceil(7.5) = 8
- 8 replicas × 12 shards = **96 nodes**

Sharding splits the data, never the query load — module 02's `shard-count` picks shards from storage and write bounds and module 06 divides load across independent servers, while here module 07's `scatter-gather` lesson becomes a fleet size.
hints: Ask what one shard sees when every query is broadcast to all of them — then size that shard as if it were the whole service.
replicas = ⌈queryQps ÷ perReplicaQps⌉; nodes = shards × replicas.
Under fan-out every shard sees the full query rate, so each shard needs ceil(queryQps ÷ perReplicaQps) copies — multiply by the shard count for the cluster

sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/08-vect.instructions:
**Skills:** search · capacity  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "We are adding semantic search over 100,000,000 chunks with 768-dimension float32 embeddings. Our search nodes have 64 GB of RAM. How many nodes does the in-memory vector index need — and what does int8 quantization buy?"

**Why it works.** Graph-based approximate-nearest-neighbour indexes keep every vector resident in RAM for the search walk. One vector costs dims × bytes per dimension (float32 = 4 bytes, int8 quantized = 1 byte), so the index holds vectors × dims × bytesPerDim (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes). Divide by one node's RAM and round up for the fleet. (Real indexes add graph-link overhead on top; this drill sizes the vectors alone.)

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `vectorBytes(vectors, dims, bytesPerDim)` → `vectors × dims × bytesPerDim`
- `vectorNodesNeeded(vectors, dims, bytesPerDim, nodeRamBytes)` → `Math.ceil(vectorBytes(…) / nodeRamBytes)`

**Worked example.** 1,000,000 vectors × 1,536 dims × 4 bytes = **6,144,000,000** bytes (~6.1 GB).
sysdrills/13-search-and-indexing/08-vect.explanation:
An in-memory graph index has no cold tail — the whole set must be resident.

For `vectorNodesNeeded(100000000, 768, 4, 64000000000)`:
- 100,000,000 × 768 × 4 B = 307,200,000,000 bytes (307.2 GB)
- ÷ 64,000,000,000 bytes of RAM = 4.8
- rounded up → **5 nodes** — or quantize to 1 byte per dimension and run 2

Module 01's `cache-working-set` keeps only the hot per-mille slice resident; here the WHOLE vector set must fit and quantization is the only discount.
hints: Unlike a cache, a graph-based ANN index such as HNSW keeps every vector resident — size for all of them, and remember nodes come whole.
bytes = vectors × dims × bytesPerDim; nodes = ⌈bytes ÷ nodeRam⌉.
An embedding costs dims × bytesPerDim and an in-memory graph index holds every vector in RAM, so multiply the three — divide by a node's RAM and round up for the fleet
